opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think what made XTX interesting was that it sat at a very unusual intersection. On one side you have a trading firm, so everything is very concrete: you build a model, you deploy it, and the market tells you very quickly whether you were right. There's no hiding behind a nice paper or a benchmark that doesn't really matter. On the other side, XTX takes research seriously and invests heavily in compute and in people who think about machine learning in a fundamental way.

For someone like me coming from mathematics, that combination was really appealing. In pure math you care a lot about rigor and about understanding *why* something is true. In machine learning, especially at scale, a lot of things work before anyone understands why. Being in an environment where you had to hold both of those attitudes at once was very formative. You learn to respect empirical results, but you also keep asking whether there's a cleaner structure underneath.

The other thing was the culture around data and signal. Financial data is extremely noisy, and the signal is tiny. That forces a kind of intellectual honesty. You become very careful about overfitting, about fooling yourself, about what really generalizes. I think that mindset carries over to almost every AI problem, including reasoning and mathematics, which is what I care about most now.

And finally, the people. You're surrounded by very sharp folks from math, physics, computer science, all trying to squeeze out understanding from hard problems. That density of talent, plus the resources to actually try ambitious ideas, made it a place where I learned a lot very fast. It also made me think more seriously about what AI could do for mathematics itself, which ended up shaping what I wanted to build next.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first of all I should say I wasn't really working on AI in the sense people usually mean. XTX is a quantitative trading firm, and the core of what they do is prediction: you have an enormous amount of market data, and you're trying to forecast where prices go in the next second, the next minute, the next hour. That's fundamentally a machine learning problem, just one with a very unforgiving teacher. The market tells you immediately whether you were right or wrong, and it tells you in dollars.

What made it interesting to me was a few things.

The first is the signal-to-noise ratio. In most ML applications, if your model is a bit off, nobody notices. In trading, you're trying to extract an incredibly faint signal from data that is almost entirely noise, and everybody else in the world is trying to extract the same signal. So any edge you find decays. You can't just train a model once and ship it. You're constantly asking, is this real, or did I just overfit to the last six months? That forces a kind of intellectual honesty that I found really healthy.

The second is scale. XTX runs on a scale of compute and data that, when I was there, was comparable to what the big labs were doing, but applied to a problem where the feedback loop is tight. In academia you might wait months to know if an idea works. There, you often know in days. That makes you learn very fast about what actually matters in a model versus what just looks elegant on paper.

And the third, honestly, was the people. It was a place full of mathematicians and physicists who had never formally studied machine learning but thought about it from first principles. They'd ask questions like, why does this architecture work at all, what's the actual statistical object we're estimating here. Coming from a math background, that was the kind of conversation I wanted to have. It made me realize that a lot of what we call AI progress is really progress in understanding optimization and generalization, and those are mathematical questions underneath.

So I'd say I went in thinking of it as a detour, and I came out thinking it had shaped how I approach AI more than almost anything else. It taught me to distrust results that haven't been tested against reality, and that's something I carry with me now.

That combination of research and practical consequences was really appealing to me.
